Deterministic policy gate, kill switch, call limits and tamper-evident audit for existing AI agent runtimes. Not an agent of its own. Models, providers and the agent loop are not reimplemented. The primary runtime is Hermes Agent (pinned at v0.23.1 for the Mac mini appliance track). Adapters can target other runtimes later. Core version 1.0.0rc1 (v1 candidate). See CHANGELOG.md , docs/v1/STATUS.md and docs/v1/INSTALLATION-AND-OPERATIONS.md . aaf-gate sits in front of tool calls and applies a deterministic policy per tool class: This is a v1 candidate (1.0.0rc1) . It is implemented and unit-tested locally. It is not production-ready , not yet device-accepted , and it makes no compliance claims . Start values for the call-limit window are assumptions in the Pilot 1 policy (3600 s; read 160, draft 40, internal_write 80) and will be reset after a pilot week from recorded gate_calls . version prints core_version , schema_version and ok as JSON. Further commands ( python3 -m framework.cli <command> ): Device installation, operation, backup and the acceptance probes are described in docs/v1/INSTALLATION-AND-OPERATIONS.md . That guide has not been executed on a device yet. Copyright 2026 Konrad Kern. Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. See LICENSE . Hermes Agent is a separate project by Nous Research, licensed under MIT. This repository contains adapter and plugin code that talks to Hermes hooks; it does not vendor the Hermes source tree. items.title: 26 AI agents rewrote a backend from Django to Rust with no human merges
items.story_key: story|title:26 ai agents rewrote a backend from django to rust with no human merges
items.content_excerpt: Pi Dash coordinated 26 Muse Code agents to rewrite its own Django backend in Rust. The main port took about ten days and cost about $350 in model usage. Pi Dash is an open source agent coordination platform developed by AI Republic, that automatically assigns tasks to a team of AI agents. We used the platform to refactor its own backend. This article is a short report on how that worked. On a Pi Dash board, agents do the issues: your own Muse Code, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor through the Pi Dash daemon, or the built-in Pi Dash Agent. The rulebook, the coordinator and the review-test-merge loop in this post are ordinary Pi Dash features. You can run the same setup on your own backlog. In late September and early October 2026, Pi Dash coordinated 26 Muse Code agents on 5 developer machines to rewrite its own backend from Python and Django to Rust. The main port took about ten days. The agents picked up issues from a Pi Dash board, wrote the code, reviewed it, tested it against the running Django server, and merged their own pull requests. The backend started as a fork of Plane ’s Django API. By September it was about 101,000 lines of application code, plus about 20,000 lines of cloud-only code. We wanted it in Rust. We also wanted to find out whether our own product could run a project this large with no person approving each step. It could, with caveats. This post covers the rules we gave the agents, how we checked that they were right, and what still needs improving. Why Muse Code and Muse Spark. Every agent was Muse Code running as a Pi Dash runner, with muse-spark-1.3-contribute as the model. We chose them for two reasons: Across the whole project, the agents sent about 166,000 requests to the model and used about 48.6 billion tokens, for a total model cost of about $350. Planning came first. Muse Code scanned the Django codebase and wrote a plan: it measured every area of the backend, marked dead code to skip, and split the rest into 10 foundation issues and 37 domain epics. Claude Code reviewed the plan. Muse Code then created the epics and the rulebook in Pi Dash through MCP, one issue per row of the plan. From there, each epic’s first run splits it into its own sub-issues, as the loop section shows. Every agent run starts by reading one rulebook, a Pi Dash issue called PIDASHCONV-1. Its main rules: The first rule fixed behavior, not code. Django does much of its work implicitly, through base classes, serializers, permission classes and lazy queryset

items.title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
items.summary: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.

items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concrete

items.title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
items.summary: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

items.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
items.summary: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.

items.title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: Now track spend by outcome
items.summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.
items.story_key: story|title:langsmith for coding agents now track spend by outcome
items.content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. items.title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
items.summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. items.title: claude-code v2.1.330
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after claude auth login, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
  • Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in /config
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1 to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --start-dir / SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
  • Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do
  • Added commandPrinted to claude plugin install --json results, true when the plugin's install command wrote to stderr, and commandFailed when it exited with an error, was killed or timed out
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_registered_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order issued to registration accepted, on orchestrator-spawned runners
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_first_session_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order to first session handed over, on runners started for a session
  • Fixed Claude Code freezing for up to several minutes right after compacting a very long conversation
  • Fixed WebFetch freezing the session for minutes on some pages, and returning an empty result for some others
  • Fixed ExitWorktree and the worktree exit dialog deleting a worktree that another running Claude Code session was working in
  • Fixed changes to user settings being lost when several Claude Code processes saved them at the same time
  • Fixed --continue and --resume opening an empty session or failing when the last saved message had a missing or invalid timestamp
  • Fixed the first prompt after a sleep of two minutes or more waiting three minutes on a connection that had died, on Linux and WSL
  • Fixed turns failing with "JSON schema is invalid", and session files growing by many megabytes, when many MCP tools have an input schema that the API refuses
  • Linux: Fixed Bash commands waiting seconds and showing no file diff for the rest of a session in slow repositories with large ignored folders such as node_modules
  • Windows: Fixed Bash commands running slower for the rest of a session after Git Bash took 10 to 60 seconds to start, on machines with no custom start-up files
  • Fixed /rewind sometimes restoring an older version of a file when two queued prompts, or stacked skills, ran together right after a turn that changed it
  • Fixed text and images added when approving a permission prompt being dropped when the approved command or tool then failed
  • Fixed MCP resources from claude.ai connectors and plugin servers not being attached when @-mentioned in the terminal's prompt box
  • Fixed an MCP server that subagents declare being shut down when one of them finished, while other subagents or the session were still using it
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome staying "not connected" after a brief connection problem, even though Chrome was open and signed in
  • Fixed terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock (Mantle) started with no model selected ignoring a pinned Opus model, and still calling an unavailable default model after announcing a fallback
  • Fixed the rest of what you were typing being lost when a plan arrived in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed claude.ai connectors with different names being dropped when they share a server URL (#101856)
  • Fixed plugins going missing from the installed list when several claude plugin commands ran at the same time
  • Fixed task dependencies and metadata being lost when several task updates ran at the same time
  • Fixed incomplete backups of ~/.claude.json being kept, and displacing good ones, when the disk was full
  • Fixed a long pause in Code Mode after code that read hundreds of files in projects with path-scoped rules or Read deny rules
  • Fixed the built-in chart tool failing when Claude called it in Code Mode
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn from a script in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Fixed Code Mode in auto mode dropping earlier thinking and rewriting the prompt cache when a mod added a note after a script loaded a skill
  • Fixed Code Mode not restoring a file that a script had read after Esc and /compact
  • Fixed /context undercounting system tools in Code Mode before Claude's first reply
  • Fixed a stopped background subagent sometimes not staying stopped
  • Fixed Claude still waiting for a background agent that was stopped just as it finished, in sessions run by an app or the SDK
  • Fixed background sessions sometimes waking in their previous permission mode after approving a plan
  • Remote Control: Fixed the note about background agents ended by a Stop from a phone or the web showing in the terminal as if you had typed it
  • Remote Control: Fixed the mobile apps hiding the Diff and pull request buttons, or showing a stopped session as working, after turning it on mid-conversation
  • Fixed environment variables written by a SessionStart hook being lost with claude -p --continue
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 with no message when its output went to a file on a full disk: it now prints an error and exits 1, though a full NFS export may go unnoticed
  • Fixed the system prompt keeping the earlier model's instructions when the model was changed after /context but before the first message
  • Fixed Claude sometimes replying to its commit attribution reminder and ending the turn early after the model changed mid-turn; it can still happen where managed settings set the PR attribution line
  • Fixed Esc not ending an LSP tool call that was waiting for a slow or stuck language server
  • Fixed LSP tool calls and diagnostics failing when several calls or edits arrived while a language server was still starting
  • Fixed /mcp listing plugin servers as built-in: they now stand under "Plugin MCPs", --mcp-config and built-in servers under "Other MCPs", and a server's page names its plugin
  • Fixed an "MCP server blocked by enterprise policy: easel" warning showing at every start when an MCP allowlist or denylist excludes the built-in chart tool, which stays blocked
  • Fixed /stats counting new activity in UTC days instead of your local time zone
  • Fixed /ultrareview failing or reviewing the wrong code after the shell moved into another repository: it now stops and names both folders
  • Fixed Grep reporting no matches when the pattern held a line break without multiline mode; it now reports the rejected pattern
  • Fixed Jupyter notebooks saved with a byte order mark being reported as invalid JSON by the Read and NotebookEdit tools
  • Fixed link reference definitions being dropped from CLAUDE.md and memory files that contain an HTML comment
  • Fixed running Monitors keeping the earlier conversation in memory until they end
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending a turn with "Prompt is too long" when a PDF larger than the context window followed a long conversation
  • Fixed the choice between two user or project agent files declaring the same name depending on the order the file search listed them
  • Fixed claude daemon logs never exiting inside a git repository when there is no log file
  • Fixed markdown hiding a character or two after bold or italic text when a backslash came before an emoji later in the paragraph
  • Fixed Edit refusing some valid hook commands in Claude settings files
  • Fixed Read with a page range showing both halves of a scanned two-page spread on each of its pages
  • Fixed line breaks and class stereotypes missing from Mermaid diagrams in HTML artifacts
  • Fixed the Project instructions picker in /config showing only one of its four choices in a 24-row fullscreen window
  • Fixed a subagent's own subagents and forks running on the plan-mode model in plan mode under opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed WebFetch page summaries ignoring the /effort level when a gateway refuses the small fast model
  • Fixed claude -p on Google Cloud's Agent Platform ignoring --settings '{"fastMode":true}' when the model comes from ANTHROPIC_MODEL or a settings file; such runs now bill at the fast mode price
  • Fixed startup under forceLoginOrgUUID being refused after one temporary server error or dropped connection
  • Fixed claude mcp remove giving no way forward for a claude.ai connector: it now says to turn it off in /mcp or remove it on claude.ai
  • Fixed the /mcp "Connect on claude.ai" check saying "not connected" when claude.ai has a connector at the server's URL without its query
  • Fixed /install-github-app and /design-login showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
  • Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
  • Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
  • Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
  • Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when --push-outcome-on-release is set
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and --startup-timeout-min is from 2 to about 6
  • Fixed pkill -f in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a pkill with --ignore-ancestors)
  • Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow spawn-runner hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
  • Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner's last_poll_age_seconds reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
  • Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with --resume, because /resume inside a running session doesn't run the task
  • Fixed claude plugin validate wrongly warning that a mod's AbovePrompt or AbovePromptList hook never runs in VS Code
  • Fixed /design-sync deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
  • Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when max_tokens exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
  • Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, claude auth login and claude setup-token: it is now much shorter
  • Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
  • Improved the speed of file diffs
  • Improved /config search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
  • Improved /resume: sessions where you only opened a screen such as /model and left are no longer listed
  • Improved Reconnect in /mcp and /plugin: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
  • Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
  • Improved /plugin in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
  • Improved /ultrareview's cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
  • Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
  • Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
  • Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a subagent's script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Changed recurring scheduled tasks and /loop to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
  • Changed more rm commands aimed at the root, home, a top-level folder or the working folder to ask for approval; where nobody can answer, they're refused
  • Changed deniedMcpServers name entries to hide only the named claude.ai connector, not others at its URL; to block them all, deny its exact URL
  • Changed claude --teleport in some setups to print the git commands for switching branch instead of running them; with -p it exits 1 until you switch
  • Changed unrecognized model names containing "sonnet" or "haiku" to use the shorter system prompt, like other unrecognized names; CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 gives every model the full one
  • Changed skills that Claude runs with a model setting, other than context: fork skills, to leave subagents, forks, compaction and /recap on the session's model
  • Changed a subagent's model fallback to carry over: agents with no model and forks it then starts run on the fallback, and the agents they start use its Bedrock region
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed spawn-runner hooks to start while earlier ones still run, up to --hook-concurrency per orchestrator (4 by default); set it to 1 if yours can't run beside another
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Bash commands to skip the file diff when nothing needs it, so transcripts can lack it; set bashEditDiffEnabled to true in managed settings to get every diff
  • Changed self-hosted runners to stop a session's start at once, without trying other runners, when a checkout hook exits with status 108
  • Changed prompt hooks to accept model aliases such as haiku or sonnet in their model field
  • Changed /design-sync's fallback build of the reference Storybook to use only a Storybook installed in the project
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions signed in to a Claude apps gateway to be written from short notes instead of the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • [VSCode] Added /fork to fork a conversation after its last reply (#69272)
  • [VSCode] Added /workflows, which opens the agent map with running workflows
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.escapeStopsClaude setting; turn it off so Escape does not stop Claude (#91536)
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.pinPrompt setting to let your message scroll away instead of staying pinned
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.contextUsageThreshold setting for when the context indicator shows (#93036)
  • [VSCode] Added a prompt argument to the "Open in Side Bar" command for keybindings and extensions
  • [VSCode] Added Move up and Move down to a session group's menu (#98654)
  • [VSCode] Fixed VS Code opening and focusing its terminal on every prompt of a connected terminal session
  • [VSCode] Fixed copying a code block adding a trailing newline that ran the command on paste (#96976)
  • [VSCode] Fixed holding Enter on /rewind restoring files, and a double click on Remove or Delete removing a memory, MCP server or plugin marketplace, without confirmation
  • [VSCode] Fixed Enter on a question card sending your earlier answer instead of picking the focused one, and arrow keys not working after an "Other" answer; answered questions reopen on your pick
  • [VSCode] Fixed a held-down Enter key sending a half-written message or running a typed slash command
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+A, C, V, X and Z not working in the rename box and dialogs on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+F and Ctrl+P not moving the caret in the message box on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Accept and Reject buttons doing nothing on a proposed diff moved to a new window
  • [VSCode] Fixed Accept and Reject Proposed Changes showing over the chat, the terminal tab and other files; they now show only on the proposed diff
  • [VSCode] Fixed a slow-starting Claude tab taking the keyboard away from the file you had gone on typing in
  • [VSCode] Fixed unsaved changes and new problems being missed on macOS and Linux for files whose path contains #, ? or %20, such as a C# folder
  • [VSCode] Fixed whole-line selections counting one line too many in the selection chip, in @-mentions and in what Claude is told, and file links leaving out the last line of a range
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation forked in the panel re-running an old, unanswered prompt by itself after a window reload
  • [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation running the original conversation's /loop schedules a second time
  • [VSCode] Fixed /clear giving no sign that the session still runs without a newly trusted folder's CLAUDE.md and settings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dialogs closing, and losing typed text, when a text selection was dragged past their edge
  • [VSCode] Fixed advisor calls showing as "Unsupported content type" (#73499, #64158, #90471, #73637)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the session list showing no status for the sidebar chat's session (#93898)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the plan preview's Add Comment button vanishing after a fast double click on a word
  • [VSCode] Fixed long lines cut off in the Edit Notebook Cell row, permission rules squeezed in a narrow panel, hard-to-see question card marks, and menus moving the chat after a declined trust prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed signing in to an account on hold showing a generic failure instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link

items.title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
items.summary: Self-hosting LLMs on GPUs means paying to recompute the same context on every turn. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut inference cost by up to 40% and time to first token by up to 80%. This post walks through the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which evaluates and sets up the cache from your coding agent.
